sections.html:
Savage sits in Scott County on the south bank of the Minnesota River, about 15 miles south-southwest of downtown Minneapolis. The river bounds it on the north, and the Credit River runs north through town to meet it. The city covers 15.61 square miles of land.

Growth came after Highway 13 was upgraded in the 1980s and the Bloomington Ferry Bridge opened in 1996. The population was 26,911 in 2010 and 32,465 in 2020, and the July 1, 2025 estimate is 32,970. Savage skews toward families: households average 2.74 people and a quarter of residents are under 18.

Most Savage homes are lived in by their owners, 85.8 percent, and about 93 percent of residents stayed in the same house over the previous year. People tend to stay, so many sales here are family moves, estates, or houses that have gone a long time without major updates.

Highway 13 and County Road 42 carry most traffic across Savage, while I-35W and U.S. 169 pass just outside the borders. Undeveloped land, including parts of the Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge and the Murphy-Hanrehan Park Reserve, is a selling point for homes near the edges of town.

Three school districts serve Savage, and that is easy to overlook when you describe a house:

  • Prior Lake-Savage District 719, with Redtail Ridge, Hamilton Ridge and Glendale elementary schools feeding Prior Lake High School.
  • Burnsville-Eagan-Savage District 191, with Harriet Bishop and Hidden Valley elementaries and Eagle Ridge Middle School feeding Burnsville High School.
  • Shakopee District 720.

Buyers ask which district covers an address, so confirm it before you list.

Registration is mandatory and free. Savage's residential rental ordinance, Title 11, Chapter 121, requires owners to register so the city and emergency services have a contact for each rental. The city ties the program to Crime Free Residential Rental Property training offered at several Minnesota locations.

An owner of a rental who plans to sell can do three things:

  • Read the ordinance before you fill out the form.
  • Ask the city how to close out or update your registration once the house is sold.
  • Pass the registration and training information to the buyer so they can register under their own name.

Timing matters when a tenant is in place. Tell the buyer early whether the tenant stays, and have the registration paperwork and training information in one folder. A buyer who plans to move in will want a different timeline than one who plans to rent the house out. The city's property protection pages are the place to start with questions.

sections.h2: Scott County property taxes and appeals
sections.html:
The second half of the property tax is due October 15. Owners pay through eNotices Online (a $1.50 charge for an e-check, 2.3 percent for a card), by mail, in a Government Center drop box, or at a county library box in the weeks before a deadline. Property and Taxation Services is at 952-496-8115.

Postal postmarks now show the day mail is first processed, not the day it was dropped off. The county suggests paying electronically, requesting a hand postmark, or mailing several business days early.

If you think your value is too high, bring evidence such as an appraisal or recent comparable sales to the city assessor. The next stop is the open book or local board session named on the value notice, and after that the county board of appeal. Tax Court is the final stage, with an April 30 filing cutoff.

Land Records records deeds, mortgages, assignments, releases and satisfactions. The number is 952-496-8150. Plats and priority documents such as sheriff foreclosures or certificates of redemption need an appointment. Electronic, mail and drop-box recordings are all processed.

  • Property Watch is a free service that emails the owner when any document is recorded under their name and parcel number.
  • RecordEASE is the paid portal for searching documents by parcel, by document number, by plat or lien, or by tract index.
  • Staff check that a document is in recordable form but can't supply legal forms or advice. They point people to the state's Uniform Conveyancing Blanks, an attorney or a title company.

Sign up for Property Watch before closing, because it shows you the day the deed is recorded. If the deed or a release seems slow, call the office and ask whether the document is waiting in the queue or needs an appointment.

State law ties homestead status to the certificate of value. A sale above $3,000 requires one at the auditor's office when the deed is recorded, and without it the property can't be classified as homestead (Minn. Stat. 272.115).

The assessor also removes the homestead classification for the next assessment year when a property sells, unless the new owner completes a homestead application and qualifies. Scott County's Taxation page explains the requirements and takes the application materials. A buyer who forgets the application can face a higher tax bill the following year, which is worth raising during negotiations.

sections.h2: What to do first when a Savage house needs to sell quickly
sections.html:
A short list of local checks saves time once you decide to move.

  1. Find your parcel number on the Scott County property information site and print the current tax statement.
  2. Confirm which of the three school districts covers the address.
  3. Check whether a rental registration is on file with the city and whether any document is waiting to be recorded.
  4. Ask a title company or attorney to prepare the deed on a Uniform Conveyancing Blank, since the county doesn't.

After that, choose a route. A listing brings showings, a buyer's loan and an appraisal, which suits a house in good shape. A cash sale skips those steps, so the schedule depends on title work and the recording paperwork. A house with deferred repairs, a tenant or an estate history can go to a buyer willing to take it in its present condition, and the same parcel records and tax statement will serve either route.

faqs.q: Does Savage charge to register a rental property?
faqs.a: No. Registration is free, but it is mandatory under Title 11, Chapter 121 of the city code.

faqs.q: Which school district serves my Savage house?
faqs.a: It depends on the address. Prior Lake-Savage District 719, Burnsville-Eagan-Savage District 191 and Shakopee District 720 all cover parts of the city, so confirm with the districts before you advertise.

faqs.q: How do I get alerts when a document is recorded on my Savage property?
faqs.a: Sign up for Scott County's Property Watch. It is free and needs only your name, property ID and email address, and it sends an alert when a document with your name and parcel number is recorded.

faqs.q: Can I still appeal my Scott County valuation this year?
faqs.a: The Minnesota Tax Court is the last step, with a cutoff of April 30 of the payable year. The meetings named on your value notice come first, so read the notice each spring.

faqs.q: What won't the Scott County Land Records office do?
faqs.a: It won't provide legal forms, help completing them or legal advice. Staff refer people to an attorney, a title company, or the state's Uniform Conveyancing Blanks.
